# 2 Kings 21 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Overview

The chapter records the reigns of two wicked kings of Judah: Manasseh (55 years, vv. 1–18) and his son Amon (2 years, vv. 19–26). The theological purpose of the chapter, according to the Deuteronomistic historian, is to explain why Jerusalem eventually fell to Babylon: the sins of Manasseh were so deep and irreversible that exile became inevitable (cf. 2 Kings 24:3–4).

**Ligonier (Reformed)** notes that 1–2 Kings, written to the exiles in Babylon, focuses on the negative — emphasising the idolatry that led to exile — while 1–2 Chronicles, written to the post-exilic community, includes Manasseh's repentance to offer hope of restoration. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/manassehs-repentance

---

## v. 1 — *Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem fifty-five years. His mother's name was Hephzibah.*

**Manasseh's birth and the extra years of Hezekiah.** Manasseh was born three years after Hezekiah's recovery from his mortal illness (2 Kings 20:6). David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic) observes: "Those additional fifteen years that Hezekiah prayed for brought Judah one of its worst kings." He quotes Knapp: "Had this good king been able to foresee the wickedness of his unworthy son, he would doubtless have no desire to recover from his sickness." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Spurgeon (Baptist)** adds a pastoral caution: "I am not sure that we should be so eager for such an extension of earthly existence either for ourselves or for others." He notes that Manasseh, born to a godly father, proves that "grace does not run in the blood; and the best of parents may have the worst of children." He also observes that twelve was "too early for a youth to reign over any nation," a perilous age for such power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-21-commentary

**Henry Morris**, quoted at Precept Austin, offers a different perspective: Manasseh's birth was necessary to preserve the Davidic line and thus fulfil God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Without Hezekiah's extension of life, the Messianic line would have been broken. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-21-commentary

**Gill (older Baptist)** notes a Jewish tradition that Manasseh's mother Hephzibah (meaning "my delight is in her," Isaiah 62:4) was the daughter of the prophet Isaiah — though this is speculative. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

**Ellicott (Anglican)** notes that Manasseh was a tributary to Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, and that his name (along with Amon) suggests Egyptian influence, reflecting the political currents of the period. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Precept Austin** notes that the 55-year reign was the longest of any Judean king, demonstrating both God's patience and the deep corruption wrought by extended wickedness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-21-commentary

---

## v. 2 — *And he did evil in the sight of the LORD by following the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.*

**The standard Deuteronomic verdict.** Guzik notes that Manasseh imitated both the Canaanites' sins and those of the Northern Kingdom. "Since God brought judgment on these groups for their sin, casting them out of their land, similar judgment against an unrepentant Judah should be expected." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Ellicott** suggests Manasseh acted "under the pernicious influence of his courtiers" — the old idolatrous nobility who had chafed under Hezekiah's reforms and used the young king's accession to reassert their influence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 3 — *For he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had destroyed, and he raised up altars for Baal. He made an Asherah pole, as King Ahab of Israel had done, and he worshiped and served all the host of heaven.*

**Reversal of Hezekiah's reforms.** Guzik: "Repentance, reform, and revival are not permanent standing conditions. What is accomplished at one time can be opposed and turned back at another time." Manasseh deliberately undid his father's godly work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Comparison to Ahab.** By explicitly comparing Manasseh to Ahab of Israel — the worst of the northern kings — the writer signals the severity of his apostasy. Guzik remarks: "Manasseh did not want to imitate his godly father. Instead, he imitated one of the very worst kings of Israel."

**Star worship.** Ellicott notes that "the Babylonian star-worship and astrology, with concomitant superstitions, had been introduced under Ahaz" and was now revived. This reflects the rising influence of Assyro-Babylonian culture during Manasseh's reign. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Gill** identifies "all the host of heaven" as the sun, moon, and stars, "particularly the planets Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, and Venus." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 4 — *Manasseh also built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, "In Jerusalem I will put My Name."*

**Defilement of the temple.** Ellicott explains that "he built altars — i.e., idolatrous altars" in the temple itself. The reference to God placing His Name in Jerusalem (1 Kings 14:21; Deuteronomy 12:5) heightens the offence: Manasseh erected pagan altars in the very place God had designated as uniquely His. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Gill** specifies that these altars were placed "in the holy place, as distinct from the courts in the next verse," making the violation even more egregious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

**Guzik** traces a tragic progression of sin: "idolatry first tolerated, then promoted, then state-funded, then true worship undermined, and finally worshippers of God persecuted and murdered." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

---

## v. 5 — *In both courtyards of the house of the LORD, he built altars to all the host of heaven.*

**Ellicott** notes that the altars were placed "even in the inner and more sacred court, where the sacrifices were offered to Jehovah." The astral cults were given space in the very precincts of Yahweh worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Gill** adds that the nobles who had resented Hezekiah's reformation "took the advantage of his youth, and advised him to these idolatries." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 6 — *He sacrificed his own son in the fire, practiced sorcery and divination, and consulted mediums and spiritists. He did great evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger.*

**Child sacrifice to Molech.** Guzik: "Manasseh sacrificed his own son to the Canaanite god Molech, who was worshipped with the burning of children." Ellicott adds that the LXX reads "his sons" (plural), and Chronicles confirms multiple children were sacrificed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Occult practices.** Guzik: "Manasseh invited direct Satanic influence by his approval and introduction of these occult arts." Ellicott notes that Manasseh "made a necromancer — i.e., formally appointed such a person as a court official" — occultism became state policy.

**Ellicott** quotes Prof. Robertson Smith: "In the time from Manasseh onwards, Moloch-worship and worship of the Queen of Heaven appear as prominent new features of Judah's idolatry. It is also probable that the local high places took on their restoration a more markedly heathenish character than before." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Gill** notes these practices were all explicitly forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 7 — *Manasseh even took the carved Asherah pole he had made and set it up in the temple, of which the LORD had said to David and his son Solomon, "In this temple and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will establish My Name forever."*

**The climax of impiety.** Ellicott: "It is meant that the Asherah was erected within the Temple itself, probably in the holy place — an act which was the climax of Manasseh's impiety." This verse deliberately echoes God's promises to David and Solomon (1 Kings 8:16; 9:3) to underline the enormity of the offence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Guzik** is blunt: "Asherah was the Canaanite goddess of fertility, and worshipped through ritual prostitution. This means that Manasseh made the temple into an idolatrous brothel." He quotes Clarke: "Asherah was no other than Venus; the nature of whose worship is plain enough from the mention of whoremongers and prostitutes." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Gill** notes that the "graven image" was set up in the house "of which the Lord said to David, and to Solomon his son" — the very temple dedicated to Yahweh's name now housed an idol. He references the theory that this image had four faces, perhaps an attempt to rival the cherubim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 8 — *"I will never again cause the feet of the Israelites to wander from the land that I gave to their fathers, if only they are careful to do all I have commanded them—the whole Law that My servant Moses commanded them."*

**Conditional promise.** Ellicott notes the allusion to 2 Samuel 7:10: the permanent possession of the Promised Land depends on permanent adherence to Yahweh alone. "The reference is to the migration to Egypt" — God promises never again to send Israel into exile, but the promise is explicitly conditional. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Gill** adds: "By obedience to which they had the tenure of the land of Canaan, Isaiah 1:19." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 9 — *But the people did not listen and Manasseh led them astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.*

**The people's willing complicity.** Guzik emphasises that the blame is shared: "He was indeed a wicked king, but perhaps the greater sin was on the part of the people who accepted this seduction willingly. 2 Chronicles 33:10 says, 'And the LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they would not listen.'" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Ellicott** explains why Judah's sin was worse than the Canaanites': "The idolatry of Judah was worse than that of the Canaanites, because they worshipped only their national gods, whereas Judah forsook its own God and was ready to adopt almost any foreign cultus with which it was brought into contact (Jeremiah 2:11)." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Patterson and Austel** (quoted by Guzik): "How superficial had been the nation's compliance with Hezekiah's reforms! Without a strong spiritual leader, the sinful people quickly turned to their own evil machinations."

**Guzik** draws a modern application: "This was a transformation of the culture from something generally God-honoring to a culture that glorified idolatry and immorality. In general, we can say this happened because the people wanted it to happen."

---

## v. 10 — *And the LORD spoke through His servants the prophets, saying,*

**God's voice through the prophets.** Guzik: "When the leaders and the popular culture had abandoned God, the LORD still had a voice to Judah. He spoke by the prophets to His disobedient people." He quotes Adam Clarke: "The prophets were Hosea, Joel, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Isaiah." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Gill**, following Jewish chronology, lists Joel, Nahum, and Habakkuk. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

**Ellicott** notes that the vagueness of "His servants the prophets" (no names given) suggests the historian was summarising the substance of many prophetic addresses. He allows that Isaiah may still have been alive and protesting, but thinks "the protests in question were those of that great prophet's disciples: the style is not Isaiah's." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 11 — *"Since Manasseh king of Judah has committed all these abominations, acting more wickedly than the Amorites who preceded him, and with his idols has caused Judah to sin,"*

**Worse than the Amorites.** Guzik calls this "a remarkable achievement of evil. The Amorites were among the Canaanite tribes who populated the Promised Land before Israel captured it, and they were infamous for their violent, immoral, and depraved culture." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Ellicott** notes that "Amorites" is used as a general designation for all the native Canaanite races, like "Achaeans" for Greeks in Homer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 12 — *"…this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Behold, I am bringing such calamity upon Jerusalem and Judah that the news will reverberate in the ears of all who hear it.'"*

**Tingling ears.** Ellicott explains the metaphor: "The dreadful news shall affect him like a sharp piercing sound" — the same figure used in 1 Samuel 3:11 and Jeremiah 19:3 for especially severe judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Gill** comments: "It will make such a noise in the world, and be so horrible and terrible; … if the report of it would be so dreadful as to make a man's ears tingle, and his heart tremble, what must it be to endure it!" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 13 — *"I will stretch out over Jerusalem the measuring line used against Samaria and the plumb line used against the house of Ahab, and I will wipe out Jerusalem as one wipes out a bowl—wiping it and turning it upside down."*

**The measuring line of Samaria.** Guzik: "God's logic is simple. If Judah insisted on imitating the sins of the Northern Kingdom, then God would answer their similar sins with a similar judgment." Ellicott connects this to Amos 7:7–9, Isaiah 34:11, and Lamentations 2:8: "The figure of the measuring line and plummet suggests the idea that Jerusalem should be levelled and 'laid even with the ground.'" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**The dish metaphor.** Guzik, quoting Wiseman: "To wipe a dish and turn it upside-down to drain signified the depopulation of the land (cf. Jeremiah 51:34)." Gill explains the image as "the emptying of Jerusalem of its palaces and houses, wealth and riches, and of all its inhabitants." Yet Gill also sees a note of hope: "the empty dish being preserved, seems to denote the restoration of Jerusalem after the seventy years' captivity." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

**Ellicott** adds a textual note: "The wiping of the dish represents the destruction of the people, the turning it upside down, the overthrow of the city itself."

---

## v. 14 — *"So I will forsake the remnant of My inheritance and deliver them into the hands of their enemies. And they will become plunder and spoil to all their enemies,"*

**Forsaking the remnant.** Guzik notes: "'Forsake' is a strong, forceful word used to describe the skinning of an animal. It is sometimes translated 'cast off'" (quoting Dilday). Ellicott concurs: the Hebrew verb is the same used in Judges 6:13 for being "cast off." The "remnant" refers to Judah and Benjamin — the Northern Kingdom had already been depopulated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 15 — *"…because they have done evil in My sight and have provoked Me to anger from the day their fathers came out of Egypt until this day."*

**Accumulated guilt.** Ellicott notes the Hebrew verb is a continuous form: "have been provoking; i.e., continually." The sin is not just Manasseh's but represents the culmination of a long history of rebellion stretching back to the Exodus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Gill** observes that Israel was "always prone to idolatry … and now the measure of their iniquity being almost up, would be reckoned for together." The golden calf episode after the Exodus is the archetype. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 16 — *Moreover, Manasseh shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem from end to end, in addition to the sin that he had caused Judah to commit, doing evil in the sight of the LORD.*

**The blood of the prophets.** Ellicott identifies the "innocent blood" as "that of the prophets of Jehovah and their followers." He quotes Robertson Smith's description of a "bloody struggle" between the conservative reactionary party and the prophetic followers, with the king siding with the reaction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Tradition of Isaiah's martyrdom.** Both Guzik and Ellicott note the Talmudic tradition (and the apocryphal *Ascension of Isaiah*) that Manasseh had the prophet Isaiah sawn in two. Hebrews 11:37 ("they were sawn in two") is widely held to allude to this. Guzik cites Wiseman: while the tradition is "uncorroborated," it is an early and persistent Jewish memory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Gill** uses the metaphor "filling a vessel brimful" to describe the extent of the bloodshed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

**Guzik** traces the tragic progression of sin in five stages: idolatry tolerated → promoted → state-funded → true worship undermined → worshippers of God persecuted and murdered → judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

---

## vv. 17–18 — *As for the rest of the acts of Manasseh … are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And Manasseh rested with his fathers and was buried in his palace garden, the garden of Uzza. And his son Amon reigned in his place.*

**Where 2 Chronicles differs.** Guzik notes that 2 Chronicles 33:11–19 records Manasseh's capture by the Assyrians, his imprisonment in Babylon, his remarkable repentance and humbling before God, his restoration to the throne, and his subsequent reforms. The Kings account omits this entirely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Why the omission?** Ligonier (Reformed) explains: "The author of 2 Kings left out the account of Manasseh's exile and repentance because he wanted to show how Manasseh's evils put the nation in a position where exile was inevitable." The Chronicler, writing for the post-exilic returnees, includes the repentance to assure them that even someone as wicked as Manasseh could be forgiven — and so could they. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/manassehs-repentance

**Guzik** applies Proverbs 22:6: Manasseh, raised by a godly father, "lived in defiance of his father's faith for most of his life. Nevertheless, at the end of his days he truly repented and served God." Yet the repentance "was too late to change the nation." Patterson and Austel suggest the occasion was the widespread revolts during Ashurbanipal's reign (652–648 BC), and "his subsequent release and reform were apparently far too late to have much of an effect on the obdurately backslidden people."

**Burial in the garden of Uzza.** Ellicott notes that this was apparently not the Solomonic palace but a separate house Manasseh built. Gill speculates that Manasseh "judging himself unworthy to lie with the kings of Judah" chose this burial location. Neither commentator reaches a firm conclusion on the origin of the name "Uzza." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## v. 19 — *Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem two years. His mother's name was Meshullemeth daughter of Haruz; she was from Jotbah.*

**Ellicott** suggests the name "Amon" may derive from the Egyptian sun-god Amen (Greek Ammon), fitting since "his father was an idolater." His mother's name Meshullemeth is the feminine form of Meshullam, meaning "friend [of God]" — a name that stands in ironic contrast to her son's apostasy. The location Jotbah is obscure; Jerome said it was in Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Gill** notes the brevity of Amon's reign: "the usual time the sons of wicked kings reigned, and instances in the son of Jeroboam, Baasha, and Ahab." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## vv. 20–22 — *And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh had done. He walked in all the ways of his father, and he served and worshiped the idols his father had served. He abandoned the LORD, the God of his fathers, and did not walk in the way of the LORD.*

**Like father, but without the repentance.** Guzik: "Amon sinned as Manasseh had sinned, without having the repentance that Manasseh repented." 2 Chronicles 33:23 explicitly states that Amon "did not humble himself before the LORD, as his father Manasseh had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Knapp** (quoted by Guzik): "There is not one bright spot in this king's character to relieve the darkness of his life's brief record."

**Trapp** (quoted by Guzik) offers the grim insight that Amon may have calculated: "My father took his swing in sin, and yet at length repented. So, thought he, will I do." This presumption cost him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Ellicott** notes that he "abandoned his worship altogether, and gave himself up to foreign superstitions which his father had introduced." The long combined reign of Manasseh and Amon (nearly 57 years) is "described by the sacred historian simply on the side of its relation to the religion of Israel." He references Zephaniah's denunciations of the same corrupt period (Zephaniah 1:4–5; 3:1–4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

---

## vv. 23–24 — *Then the servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his palace. But the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against King Amon, and they made his son Josiah king in his place.*

**Conspiracy and justice.** Guzik notes the irony: "This story of conspiracy and assassination seems to belong among the kings of Israel, not Judah. Yet when the kings and people of Judah began to imitate the sins of their conquered northern neighbors, they slipped into the same chaos and anarchy." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Ellicott** says "the servants of Amon" means "his courtiers or palace officials" — an inside job. The motive is unknown, though Patterson and Austel (quoted by Guzik) speculate it may reflect a power struggle between pro-Assyrian and pro-Egyptian factions during the waning years of Ashurbanipal's empire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21/

**Guzik** sees the people's counter-action as a hopeful sign: after tolerating nearly 57 years of wicked kings, "now it seems that they wanted righteousness and justice instead of the evil they had lived with for so long." God gave them the leaders they wanted — and now their desire had shifted.

**Gill** speculates that the people may have acted "on account of his idolatry, so depraved was the nation" — or perhaps simply to avenge the murder of their king regardless of his character. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## vv. 25–26 — *As for the rest of the acts of Amon … are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And he was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah reigned in his place.*

**Buried beside his father.** Like Manasseh, Amon was buried in the garden of Uzza rather than the royal sepulchres — a possible sign of disgrace or exclusion from the line of honoured kings. Ellicott notes he "had caused [his sepulchre] to be prepared near his father's." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Josiah's rise.** Guzik closes with a note of providence: "Though King Amon was assassinated, God did not yet allow Judah to slip into the same pit of anarchy that Israel had sunk into. Because of the righteous action of the people of the land, there was no change of dynasty, and the rightful heir to the throne of David received the throne." He quotes Dilday: "The only positive contribution Amon made to the history of Judah was to produce one of the best kings to reign on the throne of Jerusalem." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/

**Gill** recalls that Josiah had been "prophesied of by name above three hundred years before" (1 Kings 13:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/21.htm

---

## Traditions Compared

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasises that Kings was written to explain *why* the exile happened — Manasseh's sins made it inevitable. Chronicles was written to give hope to the returned exiles: even Manasseh could repent and be forgiven, so they can be too. The message is that "God's people should not fear that the Lord will be unwilling to forgive them." John Chrysostom is quoted: "If, looking to the magnitude of his own iniquities, [Manasseh] had despaired of restoration and repentance, he would have missed all that he afterward obtained." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/manassehs-repentance

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Focuses on the pastoral and evangelistic dimensions: Manasseh the sinner, the unbeliever, and the convert. Spurgeon preached on Manasseh as a model of God's converting grace: "Manasseh shall be saved … O God! my father's God! an outcast comes to thee; a hell-hound stained with blood throws himself at thy feet." The emphasis falls on God's power to save the worst of sinners — yet also on the truth that "grace does not run in the blood." https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-21-commentary

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik):** Emphasises the spiritual warfare dimension — occult practices "invited direct Satanic influence" — and the principle that cultural transformation happens "because the people wanted it to happen." Guzik draws direct applications about revival not being permanent, and about how quickly a nation can turn from righteousness to rebellion.

**Older Anglican (Ellicott):** Focuses on historical and textual detail — Assyrian political context, the meaning of Hebrew idioms, the critical question of whether the Manasseh repentance narrative in Chronicles is "genuine history" (which Ellicott affirms it "is now allowed by the best critics to be"). He connects the narrative to the wider prophetic corpus (Amos, Isaiah, Zephaniah, Micah).

**Older Baptist (Gill):** Brings in rabbinic traditions (Hephzibah as Isaiah's daughter, the specific planets worshipped) and sees typological significance in small details (the "empty dish" preserved = hope of restoration after exile). He also provides geographical and onomastic notes (garden of Uzza, Jotbah).

**Conservative Evangelical (Precept Austin/GotQuestions):** Stresses that while Manasseh's personal repentance was genuine, "he was never able to lead Judah out of the sin that he had previously led them into." The key lesson: "forgiveness does not necessarily remove the natural consequences that flow from disobedience." The long list of biblical examples of godly fathers with wicked sons (Adam→Cain, Noah→Ham, David→Absalom, etc.) underlines that "personal righteousness is not hereditary." https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-21-commentary

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes / Ellicott's critical notes):** The Ellicott commentary (though older) reflects the critical scholarly consensus that the Chronicles account of Manasseh's repentance was once dismissed as "an edifying fiction of the chronicler's" but "is now allowed by the best critics to be genuine history." The Assyrian records confirm Manasseh (Menasi/Minse, king of Yaudi) as a tributary to Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal. Some scholars date Manasseh's accession to 696 BC with a ten-year coregency with Hezekiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/21.htm

**Catholic/Orthodox:** The "Prayer of Manasseh," an apocryphal/deuterocanonical book preserved in the Septuagint but not in the Hebrew canon, claims to be Manasseh's prayer of repentance. It is used liturgically in some Orthodox traditions (e.g., at Great Compline). GotQuestions, however, judges it "highly unlikely" that the contents accurately represent Manasseh's actual prayer. Precept Austin notes the apocryphal book's existence. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-21-commentary
